name: Affect Heuristic
description: People often use an overall gut feeling to judge risks and benefits, letting a single affective impression stand in for more deliberate analysis. Things that feel good are judged as more beneficial and less risky, and vice versa.
design_relevance_note: Shows up in privacy/security prompts, AI explainability, health or fintech disclosures, and trust-building UI where tone and visual affect shift judgments before details are processed.
prevalence_note: Named explicitly mainly in behavioral-design, risk communication, trust, and safety-critical product work rather than in baseline mainstream UX teaching.

findings.description: Across two experiments, people judged the risk and benefit of a hazard as inversely related — the riskier something seemed, the less beneficial it was judged, and vice versa — even though the two should logically be independent. This inverse relationship strengthened under time pressure (which limits deliberate analytical thought), and directly manipulating people's overall affective impression of an item systematically shifted both their risk AND benefit judgments together — supporting an 'affect heuristic' where both judgments are derived from a single underlying emotional reaction rather than evaluated independently.
findings.effect_size: original inverse risk-benefit relationship: r = -.74, 95% CI [-0.92, -0.30] (per the 2022 replication's citation of the original)
findings.source_title: The Affect Heuristic in Judgments of Risks and Benefits

findings.description: Two well-powered replication studies using a more stringent analytic strategy confirmed the core inverse risk-benefit relationship across three technologies — but did not replicate one specific sub-finding: highlighting a technology's low benefits did not change risk judgments the way the original theory predicted. Risk judgments were also found to be more responsive to manipulation than benefit judgments, and the overall relationship was found to depend partly on incidental mood — a genuine partial replication, not a clean confirm or refute.
findings.source_title: Risky Therefore Not Beneficial: Replication and Extension of Finucane et al.'s (2000) Affect Heuristic Experiment
